sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

You'll learn how to ask an AI to return data in structured formats — JSON, markdown tables, bullet lists, CSV — and why this matters beyond aesthetics. Structured output is the bridge between AI and everything else: spreadsheets, databases, APIs, and automation tools.

## Why Structured Output Matters

When an AI responds in flowing prose, the output is for humans to read. When it responds in structured format, the output is machine-readable — it can be fed directly into other systems.

Consider the difference:

**Prose output:**
"John Smith is a backend developer with five years of experience who primarily works in Python. Jane Doe is a frontend developer with three years of experience in React. Marcus Lee is a DevOps engineer with seven years of experience working with AWS and Kubernetes."

**JSON output:**
The same information as a JSON array that can be imported into a spreadsheet, pasted into a database, processed by a Python script, or fed into another API call.

Structured output matters in three practical scenarios:
1. **You need to copy data somewhere else** — a table pastes directly into a spreadsheet; JSON pastes into a database import tool
2. **You need consistent format across many items** — extracting data from 50 emails in the same structure
3. **You're building an automated workflow** — a later step needs to read the AI's output programmatically

Even if you never write code, structured output is useful. A markdown table pasted into a Google Doc or Notion looks clean and is easy to read. A numbered list is easier to act on than a paragraph.

## Asking for JSON

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a standard format for structured data. You don't need to understand the technical details — you just need to ask for it and specify the fields you want.

**The prompt:**

Extract the team information from this paragraph and return it as a JSON
array. Each person should have these fields: name, role, years_experience,
primary_skills (as an array of strings).

Paragraph:
"Our team has three members: Sarah handles backend development and has
5 years of experience, primarily in Python. Marcus does frontend work,
3 years in, and specialises in React. Priya leads DevOps with 7 years
of experience across AWS and Kubernetes."
**The output you'll get:**
That output can be pasted directly into a JSON file, imported into a spreadsheet tool, or fed into a Python script. You've turned unstructured prose into structured data in one prompt.

## Asking for Tables and Lists

Markdown tables are useful when you want a visual grid you can paste into Notion, GitHub, a Google Doc, or any markdown-aware tool.

**The prompt:**

Compare these three project management tools — Trello, Asana, and Notion —
across these criteria: pricing, learning curve, best for (team size),
and standout feature.

Format as a markdown table with columns: Tool | Pricing | Learning Curve |
Best For | Standout Feature.

For numbered lists, bullet lists, or any other format, just name it:

**Numbered steps:**

Give me a step-by-step process for onboarding a new freelancer.
Format as a numbered list. Maximum 10 steps.
**Consistent bullet structure:**

List the 5 most important things to know before buying a used car.
For each item, use this structure:
- **[Item name]**: [One sentence explanation] → [One specific action to take]

**Always specify the fields you want.** "Return as JSON" alone produces whatever fields the model thinks are relevant. "Return as JSON with fields: title, summary, author, date, tags" produces exactly the schema you need. Be explicit.

## Using Structured Output for Real Work

Here are some high-value patterns you can apply immediately:

**Extract tasks from meeting notes:**

Read these meeting notes and extract all action items as JSON.
Each action item should have: owner, task, due_date (if mentioned, else null),
priority (HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW based on context).

Meeting notes:
[paste your notes here]
**Analyse a list of items consistently:**

Analyse each book title in this list and return a JSON array.
For each book, include: title, likely_genre, target_audience,
and one_sentence_description.

Books:
- Atomic Habits
- The Pragmatic Programmer
- Thinking, Fast and Slow
- Zero to One
- Deep Work
**Convert prose to CSV:**

Convert this list of contacts into CSV format with columns:
first_name, last_name, company, email (if present), role.

[paste contact list here]

**Validate before using.** AI-generated JSON sometimes has minor formatting errors — misplaced commas, unclosed brackets, inconsistent field names. Before feeding AI-generated JSON into another tool, paste it into a free JSON validator (jsonlint.com) to check it's valid. This takes 10 seconds and prevents confusing errors downstream.

sections.title: Data Extraction Pipeline
sections.content:
Open [Claude.ai](https://claude.ai) and run this three-part exercise:

**Part 1 — Extract as JSON:**
Paste this paragraph and ask for JSON output:
```
Our team has three members: Sarah (backend, 5 years experience, Python),
Marcus (frontend, 3 years, React), and Priya (DevOps, 7 years, AWS/Kubernetes).

Extract this as a JSON array where each person has fields:
name, role, years_experience, skills (array).
```

**Part 2 — Reformat as Markdown table:**
In the same conversation, ask:
```
Now reformat that same data as a Markdown table with columns:
Name | Role | Experience | Skills
```

**Part 3 — Your real data:**
Now pick something from your own work or life — a list of tasks, a set of contacts, meeting notes, a product list, a reading list. Ask Claude to extract or organise it as JSON with fields you specify.

Save the JSON output. Even if you never code, you'll find a use for it: it can be imported into Notion, Airtable, or any spreadsheet tool.
**You've completed lesson 3-6.** You can now extract structured, machine-readable data from AI output — turning unstructured text into JSON, tables, and lists that work with any other tool.
